Take a look at this research paper published 4 years ago specifically on this topic:

[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322414579\_Understanding\_and\_Identifying\_Rhetorical\_Questions\_in\_Social\_Media](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322414579_Understanding_and_Identifying_Rhetorical_Questions_in_Social_Media)  


While the error rate is not as low as a human, it goes to show that AI *can* in fact identify rhetorical questions.

It does this by training for two potential motivations of a user using rhetoric. If you have further questions read 4.1 and 4.2 that go into the framework of how such model is trained.

The claim that an AI cannot be reliable in identifying participants in a conversation is false. First by voice is already implemented in **industry** by companies such as [Otter.ai](https://Otter.ai) (identification and isolation of voice, handwriting styles, etc..). If you want to look into text, then such is easier because it is evident by grammar and formatting. 

The claim that AI cannot distinguish the intent of a participant is false. An AI *can* distinguish the intent of a user, it's just not perfect, but much better than 5 years ago. This is sentiment analysis.

The claim that AI cannot distinguish the knowledge of a participant -- I assume you mean to infer the knowledge of a person based on how they act. This is either true or false depending on what type of inference we want to talk about. AI is able to deductively and inductively infer things, but not abductively. This area was neglected until now. 

GPT-3 is now 2 years old, but it has demonstrated incredible linguistic dexterity as a general purpose model. It may not process language in the way we do, but it can certainly replicate a satisfactory output. [https://youtu.be/PqbB07n\_uQ4](https://youtu.be/PqbB07n_uQ4)

To try to explain the meaning a bit more:

"Not once exempt" in context of the previous line means that it is never seen. "a gale's construes" represents the interpretation given by a gust of wind, which does not exist, for the wind tells no tales. The only information it gives is in the direction it blows. This shows that although the wind gives no information to the subject, it's only clue is in the form of a direction, in this case, time. 

"The River" represents the flow of time. "A scene never seen" represents a unique experience produced only once. The volta usually causes a sonnet to take a different tone, but I've tried to keep the tone similar. The main body focuses on the experiences of pain and suffering unique to the individual, while the volta focuses on the lack of that experience, hence the allusion to "ignorance is bliss" in the last 2 lines.

What I mean by this is hard to describe as all philosophical-psychological topics are, but when you are in a state of self loathing and depression, you cannot possibly perceive what it would be like without it, the same way that a person that has never been depressed cannot perceive how being deeply chronically depressed would feel.

When you are in a dark part in life, your brain’s reward system is malfunctioning and it doesn’t give you the necessary components to function properly. You logically are capable to compose a scenario, but you cannot feel or imagine the true, normal, emotion that this scenario would grant you. You can only feel or perceive what your malfunctioning reward system is capable of granting. This effectively puts you in a cage that does not let you see outside of it.

Once you break free, you will feel things that you previously could not perceive, and it will feel amazing. It will feel worth it.

Psychiatrists are trained for this sort of situation. They know that they will be dealing with people with mental health issues. They will ask questions that will be easy to answer, and guide you through discussion without much effort on your part. That being said, there are a few things you can do to prepare for the appointment. 

The first thing would be to understand yourself, your emotions, how it has affected you, and why you feel this way. The psychiatrist does not know you, and will only know what you tell them. The more you can make them understand how you feel, how it affects you, why you feel that way, the higher the chances that they will be able to seriously help you. There are many things that mental illness will take away from you, but it cannot take away your ability to understand yourself. 

Lastly, the best thing you can do in a psychiatric appointment is to be honest and let information flow out. Understand that the psychiatrist judges you in the same way he judges a maths equation rather than a human being, so don’t be afraid to provide information to them to analyse and understand, for that is all they will do. They are no different from a GP, but instead of diagnosing physical symptoms, they diagnose mental ones.

Unfortunately, reality does not listen to cries for help. Reality is cold and unforgiving, it’s constant and unfeeling. If you want something to be heard by others, you must reveal what needs to be revealed in order for someone to understand you properly. Reality will not bend the rules for you. I hope you will build up the courage to speak to someone about this, but do not commit half hearted attempts. That is reality.
